title: Obtain a High Success Rate: Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction [FREE GUIDE & RESOURCE]
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Clark explains Rosenshine's seventh principle, obtaining a high success rate, which holds that effective teachers engineer lessons in which students succeed about eighty percent of the time during guided practice. He stresses, following Tom Sherrington, that this figure measures the accuracy of responses across the class rather than the share of students who understand. Too low a rate means students rehearse misconceptions, and too high means the task is too easy. He links the principle to cognitive science, where successful retrieval strengthens schema and frees capacity. The practical takeaway is to calibrate difficulty, check understanding regularly and adjust pace.
points: The eighty percent target describes overall response accuracy during guided practice, not the proportion of students who get it.
Low success rates cause students to practise and embed misconceptions, while very high rates mean little challenge.
Frequent success builds fluency, confidence and the belief that effort leads to improvement.
Each successful retrieval strengthens schema and frees working memory for more complex thinking.
Real-time checks for understanding let teachers adapt challenge and support to keep students in the struggle zone.
quotes: That sweet spot provides the right balance between security and stretch: it’s challenging enough to sustain effortful thinking, yet achievable enough for students to consolidate new knowledge and taste the joy of success.
When success rates are too low, students can rehearse misconceptions; when too high, the cognitive demand drops and it’s too easy.
When the success rate is too low, students are practicing errors and misconceptions. When it is too high, the material is probably too easy.
The Calibration: Adjusting task difficulty to stretch thinking, not measuring how many students “get it.

Rosenshine’s emphasis on a high success rate is rooted in both classroom research and cognitive science. When students experience frequent success, they build fluency and confidence, reinforcing the belief that effort leads to improvement.
Conversely, when students practise with a high error rate, misconceptions can become embedded, making future tasks harder.
